subtitle: A real lesson from the DCS Programming Course — a taste of the format.

sections.heading: Lesson Plan
sections.content:
DCS Programming Course — Lesson 1: What Is Programming? — Lesson Plan

Lesson Facts

Lesson number 1
Unit Programming as a Mindset
Suggested duration One 45–60 minute class period
Grade band Middle school / high school / both

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, learners can:

  • Explain programming in their own words as giving precise instructions in the right order.
  • Give a 5+ step instruction sequence for a simple everyday task.
  • Spot what goes wrong when an instruction is missing, wrong, or out of order.
  • Follow a set of instructions literally, without adding their own judgment.

Core Idea

Programming is giving precise instructions, in the right order, so that a “machine” does exactly what you want. A computer is not magic — it follows instructions literally, so every instruction must be exact and every step must be in the right order. In this course, the “machine” is a person.

Materials

  • Chalk and chalkboard (or a large flat stone and a stick for writing in dust)
  • Small stones or bottle caps (for marking steps on the ground, if needed)
  • Paper scraps (old notebooks, receipts, or any clean waste paper) — one piece per learner
  • A pencil or charcoal stick for each learner
  • A clear space in the classroom or outside where learners can walk safely
  • One piece of chalk or a small object (e.g., a stone, a tin can) to be “picked up” during the Human Robot activity

All materials are unplugged and village-sourced. If paper is scarce, learners can write on the ground with sticks, or use the back of old worksheets.

Lesson Outline

Opening Story — 5 minutes

Gather learners in a circle. Tell a short story:

“Imagine you ask your younger sibling to fetch water. You say, ‘Go get water.’ They come back with an empty pot. You say, ‘Why no water?’ They say, ‘You didn’t tell me where the pot was, or which path to take, or how much to carry.’”

Ask: Whose fault was it? Let learners answer. Guide them to see: the instruction was too vague. A good instruction is precise and complete.

Warm-up Game: The Human Robot — 15 minutes

  1. Choose one learner to be the programmer and one to be the robot.
  2. Give the robot a simple task: walk to the door, pick up the chalk, and bring it back.
  3. The programmer must give step-by-step instructions. The robot takes every word literally — no guessing, no filling in gaps.
  4. Example chaos: if the programmer says “walk to the door,” the robot walks to the door and stops. If the programmer says “pick up the chalk,” the robot picks up the chalk but doesn’t turn around. If the programmer forgets to say “turn around,” the robot walks backward.
  5. Let 2–3 pairs try. Each time, the class watches and laughs — but also notices what went wrong and why.

Key question after each round: What instruction was missing, wrong, or out of order?

Main Activity: The Missing Step Game — 15 minutes

  1. Write on the board a familiar task: fetching water from the well.
  2. Write the steps, but deliberately remove one step. For example:
    • Pick up the pot.
    • Walk to the well.
    • Lower the bucket into the water.
    • Pull the bucket up.
    • Walk home.
    • Pour the water into the storage pot.
  3. Ask learners to act it out. They will quickly discover the missing step: fill the bucket with water (or carry the pot carefully so it doesn’t spill).
  4. Repeat with another task: planting a row of maize. Remove a step like dig a hole or cover the seed with soil.
  5. Learners work in pairs: one writes steps, the other acts them out and finds the missing step.

Discussion — 10 minutes

Ask the class:

  • What made the robot’s task hard?
  • What happens when a step is missing?
  • What happens when a step is in the wrong order?
  • Why do we need to be so careful with instructions?

Introduce the vocabulary: program, programmer, instruction, order, run (a program). Write these on the board. Explain: when the robot follows the instructions, we say the robot runs the program.

Wrap-up and Vocabulary — 5 minutes

Review the five vocabulary words. Ask learners to say each word and give one example from today’s activities. End with a thumbs-up check: Who can explain programming in one sentence?

Assessment

During the lesson, watch for:

  • Can learners identify the missing step in the Missing Step game?
  • Can learners explain why the robot failed when instructions were vague?
  • Do learners use the word “instruction” correctly in discussion?

Quick checks:

  • Thumbs up / thumbs down: “Is ‘go get water’ a good program?” (Thumbs down — too vague.)
  • Ask one learner to give a 3-step instruction for a simple task, and have the class act it out.

Exit task (last 3 minutes): On a scrap of paper, each learner writes one instruction that would be needed to make a pot of tea. They must write at least 5 steps. Collect these to check understanding.

Differentiation

Support younger or struggling learners:

  • Pair them with a stronger partner during the Missing Step game.
  • Let them act out instructions rather than write them.
  • Use very familiar tasks (washing hands, sweeping the floor) for their first attempts.

Stretch older or stronger learners:

  • Ask them to write instructions for a task with 8+ steps, including a step that must be repeated (e.g., “stir the pot three times”).
  • Challenge them to find two missing steps in a longer sequence.
  • Ask them to explain what would happen if two steps were swapped, not just missing.

Multi-grade classes:

  • Older learners can be “programmers” and younger learners “robots” in the Human Robot game.
  • Older learners can write the instructions; younger learners can act them out.

Homework / Extension

At home: Write a program for your morning routine. Use at least 5 steps. Tomorrow, swap with a partner and follow their program exactly — no adding steps, no skipping steps. Be ready to report: Did your partner’s program work? What was missing or confusing?

Connection

This lesson strengthens algorithm design — the skill of creating clear, ordered steps to solve a problem. It also touches on decomposition, because learners break a familiar task into smaller parts. This is the foundation for Lesson 2, where learners will explore variables — the “containers” that hold the things a program works with, like the pot that holds water or the basket that holds maize.

DCS Programming Course — Lesson 1: What Is Programming? — Teacher Guide

Purpose

This first lesson opens the entire DCS Programming course. It introduces the single most important idea your learners will carry through every lesson that follows: programming is giving precise instructions, in the right order, so that a machine does exactly what you want.

In this course, the “machine” is a person. Learners will take turns being the programmer (giving instructions) and the machine (following them literally). This creates laughter, surprises, and powerful learning — because when the machine does something silly, it is almost never the machine’s fault. It is the programmer’s instructions that were missing, wrong, or out of order.

This lesson matters because it sets the tone for the whole course: programming is not about computers, screens, or typing. It is about thinking clearly. Every later lesson — variables, loops, functions, debugging — builds on this foundation. If learners understand that a program is just a precise recipe, everything else becomes easier.

Key Concepts

1. A program is a set of instructions

A program is simply a list of steps that tells a machine what to do. It is like a recipe for cooking, or directions to a village.

Say it like this: “A program is a list of instructions, written down, that tells a machine exactly what to do — step by step.”

2. Instructions must be precise

Machines (and people acting as machines) do not guess. If you say “put the pot there,” the machine does not know which pot or where “there” is. You must say “pick up the small clay pot from the shelf and place it on the ground next to the door.”

Say it like this: “A machine takes every word literally. If your instruction is not exact, the machine will do something you did not mean.”

3. Order matters

Instructions must be in the right sequence. You cannot pour water into a pot before you have picked up the pot. You cannot light a fire before you have gathered wood.

Say it like this: “The order of instructions is just as important as the instructions themselves. If you mix up the order, you mix up the result.”

4. Running a program

When a machine follows a program, we say it runs the program. In this course, when a learner follows another learner’s instructions, they are “running the program.”

Say it like this: “When the machine follows your instructions, we say the program is running. Watch what happens when it runs!”

Before You Start

The day before the lesson: - Read through this guide and the Student Handout once. You do not need to memorise anything — just be familiar with the flow. - Gather materials: chalk (for the chalkboard), a piece of string or rope (about 2 metres), a small pot or cup, a stone, and a piece of paper for each learner. - Prepare the “Missing Step” cards: write the steps for “Fetching Water” on separate slips of paper (see Answers section for the full list). You will need one set per group of 4–5 learners. - Clear a small open space in the classroom — push desks aside if needed. You need room for learners to walk from one side to the other.

On the day: - Write the word PROGRAM on the chalkboard before learners arrive. - Place the pot, stone, and string where you can reach them easily.

Teaching Flow

Opening (5 minutes)

Gather the class. Point to the word on the board.

Say: “Today we start something new. We are going to learn programming. Has anyone heard that word before?”

Let a few learners answer. Accept all answers warmly. Then say:

Say: “Programming is how we tell a machine what to do. But here is the secret: programming is not about machines. It is about thinking. And today, we are going to prove it — without a single computer.”

The Human Robot Demonstration (10 minutes)

Ask for a volunteer to be the “robot.” Bring them to the front. Place the stone on the floor near one wall and the pot near the other wall.

Say: “You are now a robot. Robots do exactly what they are told — nothing more, nothing less. They do not guess. They do not think. They just follow instructions.”

Ask the class: “What instructions should we give the robot to move the stone into the pot?” Take suggestions. The robot must follow them literally. If a learner says “pick up the stone,” the robot should ask (or the teacher can prompt): “Which stone? Where is it? Which hand?” If a learner says “walk to the stone,” the robot walks — but maybe walks past it, because no one said “stop.”

Let the class try several times. Laughter is good — it means learning is happening. After a few attempts, guide the class to produce a clear sequence:

  1. Walk to the stone.
  2. Stop.
  3. Bend down.
  4. Pick up the stone with your right hand.
  5. Stand up.
  6. Turn to face the pot.
  7. Walk to the pot.
  8. Stop.
  9. Open your hand.
  10. Drop the stone into the pot.

Say: “Look what we just did! We wrote a program — a list of exact instructions, in the right order. And the robot ran it perfectly. When something went wrong, it was not the robot’s fault. It was the program’s fault.”

The Missing Step Game (15 minutes)

Divide learners into groups of 4–5. Give each group a set of “Fetching Water” cards, shuffled. Ask them to arrange the cards in the correct order. One card is missing — they must figure out which step is missing and write it on a blank slip.

Walk around and listen. Do not give answers. Ask questions instead: “What happens if you skip that step? Would the water reach home?”

When groups finish, have each group share their missing step. Discuss why it matters.

Program Your Morning (15 minutes)

Each learner writes their morning routine as a numbered list of at least 5 steps. Remind them: be precise. Not “get ready” but “put on my shirt, then put on my shorts, then put on my sandals.”

Then learners swap papers with a partner. The partner must follow the steps exactly — acting them out silently at their desk. If a step is unclear, the partner stops and says: “I cannot run this program. Step 3 is not clear.”

Closing (5 minutes)

Say: “Today we learned that programming is giving precise instructions, in the right order. We wrote programs. We ran programs. And we saw what happens when instructions are missing or unclear. Next lesson, we will learn about variables — how machines remember things. But first, let us remember today’s lesson.”

Ask three quick questions: - What is a program? - Why must instructions be precise? - What happens if the order is wrong?

Running the Main Activity

Group sizes: 4–5 learners per group for the Missing Step game. For the Human Robot, use the whole class with one volunteer.

Timing: The full lesson takes about 50 minutes. If you have less time, cut the morning routine activity and keep the Human Robot and Missing Step game.

Common hiccups: - Learners may be shy about acting. Reassure them: everyone will take a turn being the robot or the programmer across the course. - The robot may “cheat” by guessing. Remind the robot: “You are a machine. Machines do not guess.” - Some learners may write very short morning routines. Ask them: “What would a machine need to know? Would it know how to put on a shirt?”

If learners finish early: Ask them to write a program for a task of their choice — planting a seed, sweeping the floor, greeting a visitor. The more steps, the better.

If learners fall behind: Pair them with a stronger learner. Let them work together on the morning routine. The goal is understanding, not speed.

Common Misconceptions

1. “Programming is about computers.”

Gently correct: “Programming is about thinking. Computers just happen to be very good at following programs. Today we used people as our machines — and it worked!”

2. “The machine is stupid if it does the wrong thing.”

Correct this kindly: “The machine is doing exactly what it was told. If the result is wrong, look at the instructions. The programmer must fix the program.”

3. “Instructions can be vague — people will understand what I mean.”

Use the robot demonstration as proof: “When the robot heard ‘pick up the stone,’ it did not know which stone or which hand. Machines need exact instructions.”

4. “Order does not matter much.”

Ask: “Can you put on your sandals before your socks? Can you pour water before you fetch it? Order is everything.”

Answers

Missing Step Game — Fetching Water (full sequence): 1. Pick up the empty pot. 2. Walk to the water source. 3. Stop at the water’s edge. 4. Lower the pot into the water. 5. Wait until the pot is full. 6. Lift the pot out of the water. 7. Carry the pot home. 8. Pour the water into the storage container.

Missing step (remove one of these): For example, remove step 5. Without it, the pot is lifted out empty. Or remove step 8 — the water is carried home but never poured out. Any step can be the missing one; the key is that learners notice the gap.

Morning routine — example answer: 1. Wake up. 2. Sit up. 3. Stand up. 4. Walk to the water bucket. 5. Dip the cup into the bucket. 6. Lift the cup to my mouth. 7. Drink the water. 8. Put the cup down.

Mixed-Age / Mixed-Ability Notes

  • Younger learners (12–14): Keep the Human Robot demonstration longer. Let them be the robot multiple times. Use simple tasks: walk to the door, pick up the chalk.
  • Older learners (15–18): Challenge them to write programs with 10+ steps. Ask them to include “error conditions” — what should the machine do if the pot is already full?
  • Mixed groups: Pair older with younger learners for the Missing Step game. The older learner can read the cards aloud; the younger learner can arrange them. Both learn.
  • Learners who struggle with writing: Allow them to draw their morning routine as pictures instead of words. The precision still matters — each picture is one instruction.

Extension Ideas

  • The Blindfold Walk: One learner is blindfolded. Another gives instructions to walk across the room without bumping into anything. This teaches precision under pressure.
  • Program a Song: Take a familiar clapping song. Write it as a program: “Clap twice. Snap once. Clap twice. Snap once.” Discuss how repetition makes programs shorter — a preview of loops in a later lesson.
  • Program a Recipe: Have learners write a program for making tea or porridge. Swap and follow exactly. This connects programming to cooking — and to the idea that recipes are programs.
  • The Worst Program: Ask learners to write the worst possible program for a simple task — vague, out of order, missing steps. Then have classmates “run” it and laugh at the chaos. This reinforces what NOT to do.

sections.content:
DCS Programming Course — Lesson 1: What Is Programming? — Student Handout

The Story of the Missing Salt

Amina’s grandmother taught her to cook fish stew when she was twelve. “First, clean the fish,” she said. “Then chop the onions. Then heat the oil in the pot.” Amina watched carefully and did everything just as she was told. The stew was delicious.

The next week, Amina tried to cook the stew alone. She cleaned the fish, chopped the onions, and heated the oil. But she forgot one thing — the salt. Her grandmother always added salt at the very end, just before serving. Without it, the stew tasted flat and sad.

“Ah,” her grandmother laughed. “You forgot the last step. Cooking is not just about doing things — it is about doing them in the right order, and not missing any step.”

Amina’s grandmother was teaching her something that computer scientists call programming. She just didn’t know it yet.

What We Learned

Programming is giving precise instructions, in the right order, so that someone (or something) does exactly what you want.

Think about these everyday things:

  • A recipe for porridge: Add water to pot. Light the fire. Wait for water to boil. Add maize meal slowly while stirring. Cook for ten minutes. Serve.
  • Directions to the market: Walk straight past the big baobab tree. Turn left at the red gate. Walk until you see the blue water tank. The market is on your right.
  • A clapping game: Clap your hands twice. Clap your partner’s hands once. Clap your own chest once. Repeat.

Each of these is a program — a set of instructions that someone follows to get a result.

Here is the most important idea of this whole course:

A computer is not magic. It is a machine that follows instructions literally.

This means: - If you say “pick up the cup,” it picks up the cup — not the plate, not the spoon. - If you say “walk to the door” before saying “open the door,” it will walk into the closed door. - If you forget to say “add salt,” the stew will have no salt.

A computer does not guess. It does not “know what you meant.” It does exactly what you say, in exactly the order you say it.

In this course, we do not have computers. So the “machine” will be a person — your classmate, your friend, or your teacher. You will write programs, and other people will run them. This teaches you the same thinking skills that programmers use every day, without needing any technology.

How It Works

Think of programming as giving directions to someone who has never been to your village.

Imagine you are telling a visitor how to fetch water from the river:

  1. Pick up the empty bucket.
  2. Walk out of the yard.
  3. Turn left at the path.
  4. Walk straight until you reach the big mango tree.
  5. Turn right at the mango tree.
  6. Walk down the hill to the river.
  7. Fill the bucket with water.
  8. Carry the bucket back to the house.

Now — what if you forgot step 3? Your visitor would walk straight, miss the path, and end up at the neighbour’s house. What if you said step 7 before step 1? Your visitor would have no bucket to fill. What if you said “fill the bucket” but did not say “with water”? Your visitor might fill it with sand!

This is exactly how programming works. Every step matters. The order matters. The words matter.

In this course, we will write our programs as numbered plain-language steps. Like this:

  1. Take the chalk.
  2. Walk to the blackboard.
  3. Draw a circle.
  4. Put the chalk down.

That is a program. The person who writes it is the programmer. The person who follows it is running the program.

Try It Yourself

WARM-UP (Everyone Can Do These)

Exercise 1 — The Human Robot

Work with a partner. One of you is the programmer. The other is the robot.

The robot must do exactly what the programmer says — nothing more, nothing less. The robot cannot guess, cannot fill in missing steps, and cannot do two things at once.

Program the robot to do this simple task: pick up a stone from the floor and place it on the table.

Write your program as numbered steps before you speak. Then read your steps one at a time. Watch what happens!

Hint: You will need more steps than you think. “Pick up the stone” is actually three steps: bend down, reach for the stone, close your fingers around it.

Exercise 2 — Spot the Missing Step

Here is a program for fetching water from the borehole. One step is missing. Read it carefully and find it.

  1. Pick up the empty jerry can.
  2. Walk to the borehole.
  3. Put the jerry can under the spout.
  4. Pump the handle ten times.
  5. Carry the full jerry can home.

What is missing? Write the missing step. Where should it go in the list?

PRACTICE (Core Work)

Exercise 3 — Program Your Morning

Write down the steps of your morning routine, from waking up to leaving for school. Use at least 8 steps. Be as precise as you can.

When you finish, swap your paper with a partner. Your partner must follow your steps exactly, acting them out. If your partner gets stuck, confused, or does something wrong — your program has a problem. Fix it and try again.

Remember: you are not writing what you MEANT. You are writing what you SAID.

Exercise 4 — The Wrong Order

Here is a program for making tea. The steps are all there, but they are in the wrong order.

  1. Pour the tea into the cup.
  2. Boil the water.
  3. Add sugar to taste.
  4. Put the tea leaves in the pot.
  5. Pour the hot water into the pot.
  6. Wait three minutes for the tea to brew.

Rewrite the steps in the correct order. Then act it out with a partner. What goes wrong if you follow the original order?

Exercise 5 — Too Many Words

A good program uses the fewest words possible while still being exact. Here is a program for sweeping the classroom:

  1. Pick up the broom.
  2. Sweep the floor.
  3. Put the broom back.

Is this program good enough? What is missing? Write a better version with at least 6 steps. Be exact — but do not add useless words.

CHALLENGE (Stretch Yourself)

Exercise 6 — The Blindfolded Walk

Work with a partner. One of you is blindfolded (or closes your eyes). The other is the programmer.

The programmer must guide the blindfolded partner from one side of the room to the other, avoiding three obstacles (chairs, bags, or stones placed on the floor).

Rules: - The programmer cannot touch the partner. - The programmer can only give spoken instructions. - The blindfolded partner must follow instructions literally.

Write your program first, then test it. You will probably need to revise it several times. That is normal — even professional programmers revise their work many times.

Exercise 7 — The Ambiguous Word

The word “it” is dangerous in programming. Look at this program:

  1. Pick up the cup.
  2. Put it on the table.
  3. Pick up the plate.
  4. Put it on the shelf.

Now answer: what is “it” in step 4? The plate? Or the cup?

Write a version of this program that cannot be misunderstood. Then write a short program of your own that uses “it” in a confusing way, and challenge a partner to fix it.

Exercise 8 — Program a Song

Think of a song or clapping game you know well. Write it as a program with numbered steps. Be so precise that someone who has never heard the song could perform it correctly.

Challenge: Have a partner run your program. If they make a mistake, is it their fault — or is it a problem with your program?

Words We Learned

Word What it means
Program A set of precise instructions, in the right order, to get something done
Programmer The person who writes the instructions
Instruction One single step in a program — one exact thing to do
Order The sequence of steps; changing the order changes the result
Run (a program) To follow the instructions, step by step, exactly as written

Remember

  • Programming is giving precise instructions, in the right order. Nothing more, nothing less.
  • A computer (or a human robot) takes your words literally. It does not guess what you meant.
  • Every step matters. One missing step can ruin the whole program — like missing the salt in the stew.
  • The order matters. Boiling water after pouring the tea makes no sense.
  • If the program fails, the problem is in the program — not in the machine. Fix your instructions, not your “machine.”

You have just learned the most important idea in all of computer science. Everything else — variables, loops, functions, debugging — builds on this one foundation: precise instructions, in the right order.

Welcome to programming.
